text:
Take on Irreplaceable You (2018 movie)
So, on a random Sunday, I came across this movie, and my decision to watch it was largely based on its poster. There was a cute girl sitting on the shoulders of a cute, clean-shaven guy with a very prominent dimple. What can I say? The poster did its job.
Going into the movie, I was expecting a deep, moving love story. Sam and Abbie had the history to make it one: childhood sweethearts who had been together for nearly two decades. But somehow, that love never quite translated onto the screen. Or maybe I just didn’t get it.
Abbie seemed determined to stay in control of Sam’s life, deciding who he should date, when he should move on, and even who would take care of him. Sam, on the other hand, seemed rather lost when it came to Abbie. He didn’t quite know how to support her or navigate what was happening between them.
And then there was Dominic, the nurse, who somehow seemed more emotionally invested in Abbie than Sam did.
By the end, Sam’s marriage proposal felt less like a declaration of love and more like an act of pity. Perhaps that wasn’t the intention, but that’s how it came across to me.
For a couple who had spent almost their entire lives together, I expected to feel their love. Unfortunately, I was left wondering whether I had missed something or whether the movie had.
Let me know what you think of it.

text:
External Inspiration in Cinema

I recently watched Denis Villeneuve’s Incendies and was blown away by how unusually well written and directed it was. It was like a perfect puzzle that resulted in a very strong emotional impact. Considering it’s based on a play written by a witness of the Lebanese Civil War, do you think there is a special kind of passion and inspiration coming from extreme real-life experience?

I’m not really talking about the re-telling of real dramatic events like in Warfare or Oppenheimer, but rather about how actually living through some painful and impactful stuff stimulates a special ingenuity in fiction. I’m not sure if someone not directly familiar with the subject matter could make such transcendent works as Incendies or Come and See.

Of course, there are many great films that don’t have an obvious real-life background and that still feature incredible mind-bending stories, but I feel like the real world contains much more material for creativity and storytelling than simply looking back at successful predecessors within cinema.

Especially nowadays, with the problem of constant low-quality remakes and sequels, do you think authors should pay more attention to real-life events and stories to keep providing fresh perspectives? Is cinema too fixated on itself?

text:
The Outlaw King 2018. What do you think?

If any film is worthy of standing beside *Braveheart* on the Mount Rushmore of great historical epics, it’s *The Outlaw King*.

Shot on location in Scotland, the cinematography delivers a grounded, almost tactile realism that serves as the perfect backdrop to one of history’s great unfinished stories: What happened after William Wallace was executed?

The film follows Robert the Bruce, an improbable underdog who suffers a humiliating early defeat at the hands of the English. Forced by cunning and treachery to abandon conventional warfare, the newly crowned king must fight dirty, embracing guerrilla tactics that slowly turn the tide of the war.

The battles themselves are gritty, dirty, and bloody fought at such close quarters that they generate a rising sense of claustrophobia. Like a train gathering steam, the tension builds gradually until it erupts into an unstoppable force.

Stephen Dillane is masterfully cast as King Edward I of England. His cold demeanor, calculating mind, and the quiet weight of a man who has held a feudal kingdom together through sacrifice and war radiate from the screen. Opposite him, Chris Pine surprises as Robert Bruce, Earl of Carrick. Stoic and haunted by the ghosts of what might have been, he ultimately chooses to stand against the impossible not just for himself, but for everyone’s freedom.

Everything builds to the Battle of Loudoun Hill, where Robert, outnumbered 5 to 1, faces a formidable English cavalry charge. The tactics he employs mirror the real historical strategy that broke the English momentum, much as *Braveheart* dramatized Stirling Bridge. The sequence is one of the most brutal and chaotic medieval combat scenes ever filmed—complete pandemonium, yet strangely unforgettable for any fan of medieval warfare. Watching it, you can’t help but think: *This* is what we saw in our minds as kids when we played *Age of Empires II* back in 1998.

text:
The "Rocky" franchise is the best thing for kids
I got two girls, ages 9 and 12. They knew about "Rocky" for a while and loved the theme music, but I held off on showing them the movie until this month.

They love Rocky. We've seen Rocky I-IV plus "Rocky Balboa" and they're ready to watch "Creed."

I never realized it until watching with them, but these movies tick all the checkboxes as good for kids.

The story is about a man who has nothing and nobody, but is decent, hardworking and when he gets a chance to be something else, he pours all his heart and soul into it. He never forgets his people or where he came from and always wants to help those around him.

There are no villains. The other boxers are just other boxers. Apollo Creed becomes a friend and the worst we can say about him is that he was proud enough to be a dick in order to get Rocky back into the ring. The hyper aggressive Clubber Lang never goes beyond trash talking and going all out in the ring. Even Ivan Drago, the closest thing to a villain we get, is very much a victim of the system he was born into. "Rocky IV," is a drop in quality from the movies that came before, but the story is mindful to show Drago really has little agency; his wife speaks for him, his entire life is curated and we can easily read his stoic aggression as a mask for resignation rather than enthusiasm. He notably says to Rocky, "I *must* break you." That's a wording of obligation, rather than desire.

The story goes that Dolph Lungren got the job because he was the only one who did his line reading in a robotic way while all the other actors read like pro wrestlers.

Winning isn't everything. Rocky loses the judgement in both "Rocky" and "Rocky Balboa," but winning was never the point in those stories; the fact he makes it through the end is a triumph. text:
Just watched Furiosa. Solid movie - but feels pretty underwhelming in comparison to Fury Road

A prequel about Furiosa is not really something I was ever particularly interested in, even with how amazing her character was in Fury Road. But I'll never say no to more Mad Max-related stuff from George Miller. I went into Furiosa with reserved expectations just because of the insanely high bar Fury Road set as one of the greatest action movies of all time. I don't want to turn this into a Fury Road glaze session (although it's hard not to) but given that this is a very directly-connected prequel with a lot of the same characters, you pretty much *have* to bring it up.

I think managing my expectations really did help a lot because Furiosa, while being a pretty well-made action movie, is nowhere near the level of Fury Road.

It's not *bad* or anything and there's a lot it does pretty well. Chris Hemsworth for example is amazing as Dementus and might in fact be my favourite villain of the entire franchise. It's such a fun performance - he really seems like he's having a blast. Tom Burke was very good as Praetorian Jack as well.

The movie also does a good job of deepening the worldbuilding from Fury Road and just...having more of an actual story.

In terms of the stunts and set pieces, while it doesn't really hit those Fury Road highs, there are some great ones here as well, especially the central War Rig sequence.

Now in terms of what doesn't work:

\- The pacing is really wonky. The first hour is honestly a bit of a slog. I know we had to see Furiosa develop from a child into a capable warrior but this sequence really dragged for me. Fury Road's pacing is just pitch-perfect - that movie doesn't have a single wasted second, which I didn't really feel with Furiosa. It just jumps from one plot point to the next without letting the story breathe. It feels both rushed *and* sluggish at the same time. It's really missing that purity of focus that Fury Road had

\- There was a lot of CG in this one, which I don't mind in a vacuum, but a lot of it honestly looked pretty bad and stuck out like a sore thumb

\- Anya Taylor-Joy does a good facsimile of Charlize Theron's Furiosa voice, but ultimately she just doesn't have the sauce to come off as a badass warrior like Charlize does, even as a young version of the character. Charlize Theron just has this *intensity* that I never really saw with ATJ. In fact, I got almost *nothing* from this character. She's almost a complete blank slate

So overall, this doesn't really hold a candle to Fury Road (which, let's be fair, very few action films do) but is still a pretty solid movie on its own merits.

Why this is vital viewing is because when you put all of this together and add it up in totality, you're left with this sense of a person that is very warped, depraved and very, very dangerous. text:
If you haven't watched Requiem for a Dream and are under the age of 35 or so, temper your expectations.
I just watched it for the first time. Well-made movie, unique cinematography, good acting.

But it's feeling dated. Real dated. It is now the midpoint between The Godfather Part II and the present day. And as such, it deals with the context of a very much bygone era. Don't worry, this isn't a "kids these days don't know what payphones are" rant, although the world it takes place in feels decidedly old at this point.

RfaD came out at the peak of the first wave of the opioid epidemic in the US. Definitely not a good time for many people, and the general populace was broadly aware of the problem, but it was still a sort of "underworld" that most people never felt that close to. You, person who's about to comment that they knew junkies in the 90s, are the exception - most people did not. It was something you heard about in DARE classes and the occasional celebrity overdose story. It was scary, but still mysterious, which is why RfaD was a significant movie. It laid bare that "this is happening right now in YOUR streets, this is what it looks like, and YOU need to know about it." Aside from Trainspotting, nobody had pulled back the curtains in such a raw way before. It definitely was (and still is) a sad, depressing, and disturbing story. But in 2000, you would watch that movie and go "yikes, that sure opened my eyes to the problem that is still largely happening somewhere else, to nobody I know."

Now for some perspective. We are in a different world now - it is quite literally ten times worse. Synthetic opioids are everywhere. But it's not just that more people are dying, it's the way they are dying. The people who do them are not your typical 90s junkie image of a guy covered in sores with fingerless gloves and a beanie sitting on a couch in a bare room with paint peeling off the walls and a single flickering lightbulb above. It's not back alleys and selling sex to enigmatic pimps in high rises . People don't "know a guy who's a drug addict now" anymore - again, maybe you do, but most people don't. So many victims don't get anywhere near the point in their life where they are seeing the consequences that the characters in the movie face. Fentanyl overdoses happen to the most random fucking people in your lame normal life. I was raised in a goody two shoes affluent suburb, I've never even seen hard drugs, and I know a few people who have OD'd. Last year I saw a totally put-together woman OD in her car in a Starbucks drive thru. There is no dark underbelly of society anymore; drugs these days just take people out of nowhere.

So if the current phase of the opioid epidemic is the only one you have been old enough to witness, RfaD may feel like it takes a bit too much of a bow for "how much truth it just dropped on you, man." You could be forgiven for thinking it comes off as rather quaint, and appreciating it in, well, the same way young people in 2000 appreciated The Godfather Part II. Significant, high-quality filmmaking, but very much a product of a different time.

EDIT: Guys, the whole "addiction takes many forms" thing with the mom was not lost on me. And I know the director said the movie isn't about opiates, that doesn't make it true - it's mostly about opiate addiction. I'm just saying, a lot of people talk about how this movie hit home because they knew someone who died from a heroin OD. If that happened in the 90s, then yes this movie may have been a fairly accurate (if very dramatized) representation of their life. But if that happened in 2022, there is a pretty good chance they did not lead anything close to the typical "drug addict" life you see in the movie.
